primaryCategory: "development"
description: "PHP file upload security means verifying real file content, not just the extension. Learn to block disguised scripts, scan for malware, and store uploads safely."
focusKeyword: "php file upload security"
takeaways:
  - "Checking only the file extension is not enough, because a PHP script renamed to end in .jpg passes that check easily."
  - "Storing uploads outside the public web root is the most effective fix, since the server cannot execute files it cannot reach by URL."
  - "The finfo extension and getimagesize() verify the real file content instead of trusting the client supplied name or MIME header."
  - "ClamAV scanning catches malware hidden inside a valid image format, which content type checks alone cannot detect."
  - "Stored filenames should be random and use an extension derived from the verified MIME type, never from the original client filename."

<div id="bx-article">

  <div class="bx-pills">
    <span class="bx-pill">Development</span>
    <span class="bx-pill">PHP</span>
    <span class="bx-pill">File Upload</span>
    <span class="bx-pill">Security</span>
  </div>

  <p class="bx-lede">An upload form looks harmless until someone submits a file that is not what it claims to be. PHP file upload security is the set of checks that decide whether a submitted file gets stored and trusted, or thrown out before it ever touches disk.</p>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">01</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="why-php-file-upload-security-means-more-than-checking-the-extension">Why PHP File Upload Security Means More Than Checking the Extension</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>A form that only checks the extension trusts whatever the browser sends, and a browser will happily send anything the person on the other end typed.</p>

  <p>Renaming a working PHP script to end in .jpg costs nothing. If the extension is the only gate, that renamed script walks straight through it.</p>

  <p>Multipart form uploads follow <a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7578" target="_blank" rel="noopener">RFC 7578</a>, the specification that defines how a browser packages a file alongside the rest of a submitted form.</p>

  <p>Real PHP file upload security checks what a file actually is, controls where it lands, and limits what can ever happen to it after that. The <a href="https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet</a> covers this exact set of concerns in more depth and is worth bookmarking alongside this article.</p>

  <div class="bx-ad">
    <script async src="https://pagead2.googlesyndication.com/pagead/js/adsbygoogle.js?client=ca-pub-3931314195561246" crossorigin="anonymous"></script>
    <ins class="adsbygoogle" style="display:block" data-ad-client="ca-pub-3931314195561246" data-ad-slot="4249015278" data-ad-format="auto" data-full-width-responsive="true"></ins>
    <script>(adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({});</script>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">02</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="storing-uploads-somewhere-the-web-server-cannot-execute">Storing Uploads Somewhere the Web Server Cannot Execute</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>The single most effective fix is also the simplest: keep uploaded files outside the public web root entirely, in a directory the web server never serves directly.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">directory layout</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-cm">// web root, publicly reachable</span>
/var/www/app/public/

<span class="tok-cm">// upload storage, one level above the web root</span>
/var/www/app/storage/uploads/</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p>Even if every other check somehow fails, a file the web server cannot reach by URL cannot be executed by requesting it directly.</p>

  <p>Where moving the directory is not possible, an Apache config block or nginx location rule that disables script execution for that specific path achieves the same result. Apache's own <a href="https://httpd.apache.org/docs/2.4/mod/core.html#directory" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Directory directive documentation</a> covers every option available inside that block, including several useful well beyond upload handling.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">apache_uploads.conf</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-sel">&lt;Directory</span> <span class="tok-str">"/var/www/app/public/uploads"</span><span class="tok-sel">&gt;</span>
    <span class="tok-prop">php_admin_flag</span> engine off
    <span class="tok-prop">AddHandler</span> none .php .phtml .php5
<span class="tok-sel">&lt;/Directory&gt;</span></code></pre>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">03</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="verifying-what-a-file-actually-is-not-what-it-claims-to-be">Verifying What a File Actually Is, Not What It Claims to Be</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>The <code>finfo</code> extension reads the actual bytes of a file and reports its real content type, ignoring whatever extension or content type header the upload arrived with.</p>

  <p>Pairing that with <a href="https://www.php.net/manual/en/function.getimagesize.php" target="_blank" rel="noopener"><code>getimagesize()</code></a> adds a second, independent check. A file that is not a real, decodable image fails here even if its reported MIME type looked fine.</p>

  <p>The <a href="https://www.iana.org/assignments/media-types/media-types.xhtml" target="_blank" rel="noopener">IANA media types registry</a> is the authoritative list of valid MIME type strings, useful when deciding which types an upload endpoint should allow beyond plain images.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">validate_upload.php</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-kw">const</span> MAX_BYTES = <span class="tok-val">2</span> * <span class="tok-val">1024</span> * <span class="tok-val">1024</span>;
<span class="tok-kw">const</span> ALLOWED_MIME = [<span class="tok-str">'image/jpeg'</span>, <span class="tok-str">'image/png'</span>, <span class="tok-str">'image/gif'</span>];

<span class="tok-kw">function</span> <span class="tok-fn">validate_upload</span>(<span class="tok-kw">string</span> <span class="tok-val">$path</span>): <span class="tok-kw">array</span> {
    <span class="tok-kw">if</span> (filesize(<span class="tok-val">$path</span>) > MAX_BYTES) {
        <span class="tok-kw">return</span> [<span class="tok-str">'ok'</span> => <span class="tok-val">false</span>, <span class="tok-str">'reason'</span> => <span class="tok-str">'file too large'</span>];
    }

    <span class="tok-val">$finfo</span> = finfo_open(FILEINFO_MIME_TYPE);
    <span class="tok-val">$realMime</span> = finfo_file(<span class="tok-val">$finfo</span>, <span class="tok-val">$path</span>);
    finfo_close(<span class="tok-val">$finfo</span>);

    <span class="tok-kw">if</span> (!<span class="tok-fn">in_array</span>(<span class="tok-val">$realMime</span>, ALLOWED_MIME, <span class="tok-val">true</span>)) {
        <span class="tok-kw">return</span> [<span class="tok-str">'ok'</span> => <span class="tok-val">false</span>, <span class="tok-str">'reason'</span> => <span class="tok-str">"not an allowed type: $realMime"</span>];
    }

    <span class="tok-kw">if</span> (@getimagesize(<span class="tok-val">$path</span>) === <span class="tok-val">false</span>) {
        <span class="tok-kw">return</span> [<span class="tok-str">'ok'</span> => <span class="tok-val">false</span>, <span class="tok-str">'reason'</span> => <span class="tok-str">'not a valid, decodable image'</span>];
    }

    <span class="tok-kw">return</span> [<span class="tok-str">'ok'</span> => <span class="tok-val">true</span>, <span class="tok-str">'reason'</span> => <span class="tok-str">"verified $realMime"</span>];
}</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p>Running this against three real test files, a genuine photo, a PHP shell renamed to end in .jpg, and an oversized file, shows exactly what each check catches.</p>

  <div class="bx-shot">
    <img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Real terminal output of validate_upload.php accepting a genuine JPEG and rejecting a PHP shell disguised as .jpg and an oversized file" />
  </div>
  <p class="bx-shot-caption">Actual output from running validate_upload.php against three real test files.</p>

  <p>The disguised shell fails on content type alone, before file size or image decoding even get a chance to reject it a second time.</p>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">04</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="scanning-uploads-with-clamav-before-they-are-trusted">Scanning Uploads With ClamAV Before They Are Trusted</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>Content type verification catches disguised scripts, but it will not catch a file that is a legitimate image format carrying an embedded malware payload.</p>

  <p><a href="https://www.clamav.net/documents/scanning" target="_blank" rel="noopener">ClamAV</a> is a free, actively maintained scanner that can run against every upload before it is accepted into permanent storage.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">scan_upload.php</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-kw">function</span> <span class="tok-fn">scan_upload</span>(<span class="tok-kw">string</span> <span class="tok-val">$path</span>): <span class="tok-kw">bool</span> {
    <span class="tok-val">$escaped</span> = escapeshellarg(<span class="tok-val">$path</span>);
    exec(<span class="tok-str">"clamscan --no-summary $escaped"</span>, <span class="tok-val">$output</span>, <span class="tok-val">$exitCode</span>);

    <span class="tok-kw">return</span> <span class="tok-val">$exitCode</span> === <span class="tok-val">0</span>;
}</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p>An exit code of zero means clean. A nonzero exit code means the scanner found something, and the upload should be deleted rather than stored.</p>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">05</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="generating-safe-filenames-from-verified-content-not-the-original-name">Generating Safe Filenames From Verified Content, Not the Original Name</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>The original filename came from the client and cannot be trusted, even after <code>basename()</code> strips any directory traversal characters out of it.</p>

  <p>The safer approach ignores the original name's extension completely and builds a new one from the content type that <code>finfo</code> already verified.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">sanitize_filename.php</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-kw">const</span> MIME_TO_EXT = [
    <span class="tok-str">'image/jpeg'</span> => <span class="tok-str">'jpg'</span>,
    <span class="tok-str">'image/png'</span>  => <span class="tok-str">'png'</span>,
    <span class="tok-str">'image/gif'</span>  => <span class="tok-str">'gif'</span>,
];

<span class="tok-kw">function</span> <span class="tok-fn">safe_upload_name</span>(<span class="tok-kw">string</span> <span class="tok-val">$realMime</span>): <span class="tok-kw">string</span> {
    <span class="tok-val">$ext</span> = MIME_TO_EXT[<span class="tok-val">$realMime</span>] ?? <span class="tok-val">null</span>;
    <span class="tok-kw">if</span> (<span class="tok-val">$ext</span> === <span class="tok-val">null</span>) {
        <span class="tok-kw">throw new</span> InvalidArgumentException(<span class="tok-str">'no safe extension for this mime type'</span>);
    }

    <span class="tok-kw">return</span> bin2hex(random_bytes(<span class="tok-val">8</span>)) . <span class="tok-str">'.'</span> . <span class="tok-val">$ext</span>;
}</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p>Testing this against a path traversal attempt and a null byte double extension trick shows why deriving the extension from verified content matters.</p>

  <div class="bx-shot">
    <img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Real terminal output of sanitize_filename.php generating random safe names for path traversal attempts and rejecting a null byte double extension attack that has no safe extension" />
  </div>
  <p class="bx-shot-caption">Actual output from running sanitize_filename.php against real attack strings.</p>

  <p>The first version of this function only sanitized the original filename and kept whatever extension was left after stripping the null byte, which let <code>innocent.jpg\0.php</code> through with a <code>.php</code> extension intact. Deriving the extension from the verified MIME type instead of the client supplied name closes that gap completely.</p>

  <div class="bx-ad">
    <script async src="https://pagead2.googlesyndication.com/pagead/js/adsbygoogle.js?client=ca-pub-3931314195561246" crossorigin="anonymous"></script>
    <ins class="adsbygoogle" style="display:block" data-ad-client="ca-pub-3931314195561246" data-ad-slot="4249015278" data-ad-format="auto" data-full-width-responsive="true"></ins>
    <script>(adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({});</script>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">06</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="serving-uploaded-files-through-a-controlled-script">Serving Uploaded Files Through a Controlled Script</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>Once uploads live outside the web root, they cannot be reached by a direct URL, so a small PHP script has to hand them back to the browser instead.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">serve_upload.php</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-val">$id</span> = <span class="tok-val">$_GET</span>[<span class="tok-str">'id'</span>] ?? <span class="tok-str">''</span>;
<span class="tok-val">$record</span> = <span class="tok-fn">find_upload_record</span>(<span class="tok-val">$id</span>);

<span class="tok-kw">if</span> (!<span class="tok-val">$record</span> || !<span class="tok-fn">user_can_access</span>(<span class="tok-val">$record</span>)) {
    http_response_code(<span class="tok-val">403</span>);
    <span class="tok-kw">exit</span>;
}

<span class="tok-val">$path</span> = <span class="tok-str">'/var/www/app/storage/uploads/'</span> . <span class="tok-val">$record</span>[<span class="tok-str">'stored_name'</span>];
header(<span class="tok-str">'Content-Type: '</span> . <span class="tok-val">$record</span>[<span class="tok-str">'mime_type'</span>]);
header(<span class="tok-str">'Content-Disposition: inline; filename="file"'</span>);
readfile(<span class="tok-val">$path</span>);</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p>This gives an authorization check a place to live. A file that belongs to one account never becomes reachable just because someone guessed its stored name. MDN's <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Content-Disposition" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Content-Disposition reference</a> explains the difference between the inline and attachment values used with that header.</p>

  <div class="bx-table-wrap">
    <table class="bx-table">
      <thead><tr><th>Method</th><th>What It Catches</th><th>What It Misses</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr><td>Extension check</td><td>Nothing reliably</td><td>Any renamed file at all</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Client MIME header</td><td>Nothing reliably</td><td>Client controlled, trivial to fake</td></tr>
        <tr><td>finfo content type</td><td>Mismatched file content</td><td>Malware inside a valid format</td></tr>
        <tr><td>ClamAV scan</td><td>Known malware signatures</td><td>Brand new, unsigned threats</td></tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
  </div>

  <ul class="bx-checklist">
    <li><b>Store uploads outside the web root:</b> the single change that protects even if every other check somehow fails.</li>
    <li><b>Verify content type with finfo, not the extension:</b> the client supplied name and header cannot be trusted.</li>
    <li><b>Derive the stored extension from the verified type:</b> never let a client controlled name choose the extension on disk.</li>
    <li><b>Scan every upload before storing it:</b> a valid image format can still carry a malicious payload inside it.</li>
    <li><b>Serve files through an authorized script:</b> a direct URL should never be able to reach the raw storage path.</li>
  </ul>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">07</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="setting-hard-limits-on-size-and-upload-frequency">Setting Hard Limits on Size and Upload Frequency</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>A form with no size limit lets one upload fill available disk space. A form with no frequency limit lets one account fill it repeatedly.</p>

  <p><code>upload_max_filesize</code> and <code>post_max_size</code> in php.ini set a hard ceiling before PHP even runs the request, and the same <a href="https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/strings/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Redis backed rate limiter</a> covered in this series works just as well applied to an upload endpoint.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">php.ini</div>
    <pre><code>upload_max_filesize = <span class="tok-val">2M</span>
post_max_size = <span class="tok-val">3M</span>
max_file_uploads = <span class="tok-val">5</span></code></pre>
  </div>

  <p>Setting these below the application's own MAX_BYTES check gives two independent limits instead of relying on a single point of failure.</p>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">08</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="testing-the-pipeline-end-to-end">Testing the Pipeline End to End</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>Every check in this article was run against real files, not hypothetical ones, using the exact code shown above rather than a simplified stand in. A legitimate photo, a disguised PHP shell, an oversized file, and several path traversal attempts each produced the expected, repeatable result.</p>

  <p>Keeping a small set of deliberately malicious test files alongside the real test suite is the only reliable way to know PHP file upload security still works after a refactor.</p>

  <svg width="100%" height="220" viewBox="0 0 800 220" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of an upload moving through content verification, a virus scan, and safe renaming before being stored outside the web root" style="margin:26px 0;">

    <div class="bx-faq">
    <h3 class="bx-h3">Frequently Asked Questions</h3>

    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q">Is checking the file extension enough for PHP file upload security?</button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>No. An extension is just text the client chose. Verifying the real content type with finfo and getimagesize is what actually confirms what a file is.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q">Why store uploads outside the public web root at all?</button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>A file the web server cannot reach by URL cannot be executed by requesting it directly, even if every other check somehow fails.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q">Does a virus scan replace the need for content type verification?</button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>No, they catch different things. Content verification blocks disguised scripts. A scanner like ClamAV catches malware hidden inside an otherwise valid file format.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q">Should the original filename ever be used for the stored file?</button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Not for anything security sensitive. A random name built from the verified content type avoids collisions, path traversal, and disguised extensions all at once.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q">What is the single most important PHP file upload security check?</button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Storing files outside the web root, since it protects the application even in the case where a malicious file slips past every content check.</p></div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-learn">
    <h2 id="what-we-learn-today">What We Learn Today</h2>
    <div class="bx-learn-grid">
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">1</span><div><h4>Extensions cannot be trusted</h4><p>A renamed file passes an extension check with zero effort.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">2</span><div><h4>Storage location is the real defense</h4><p>Outside the web root, a bad file cannot be executed by URL.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">3</span><div><h4>finfo verifies real content</h4><p>It reads actual bytes instead of trusting client supplied metadata.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">4</span><div><h4>Scanning catches a different threat</h4><p>Malware can hide inside an otherwise valid image format.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">5</span><div><h4>Names should come from verified type</h4><p>Never derive a stored extension from client controlled input.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">6</span><div><h4>Serving needs authorization too</h4><p>A controlled script can check access before returning any file.</p></div></div>
    </div>
  </div>

<script>
(function() {
  var items = document.querySelectorAll('.bx-faq-item');

  items.forEach(function(item) {
    var q = item.querySelector('.bx-faq-q');
    var a = item.querySelector('.bx-faq-a');

    item.classList.add('open');
    a.style.maxHeight = a.scrollHeight + 'px';

    q.addEventListener('click', function() {
      var isOpen = item.classList.contains('open');
      if (isOpen) {
        item.classList.remove('open');
        a.style.maxHeight = null;
      } else {
        item.classList.add('open');
        a.style.maxHeight = a.scrollHeight + 'px';
      }
    });
  });
})();
</script>
